blocks.text: 1. overview

blocks.alt: If A is bought, confidence measures how often B is also bought

blocks.text: Support, the previous topic, measures how often an entire itemset occurs together, but it is fundamentally a non-directional measurement: the support of bread, butter, and jam appearing together is exactly the same number whether the rule under consideration is bread and butter implies jam, or jam implies bread and butter. Confidence, the second of the three core metrics used to score association rules, answers a sharper, genuinely directional question instead: given that a customer already bought the antecedent, how often did they also go on to buy the consequent?

This directional framing is exactly what a useful association rule needs to capture, since a rule is, at its heart, a directional prediction, if this happens, that tends to follow, not merely an observation that two things sometimes occur together. Confidence gives that directional prediction a precise, quantifiable strength.
2. The Formula

blocks.alt: Support of A and B together over support of A alone gives the confidence value

blocks.text: For a rule of the form bread and butter implies jam, Confidence is calculated as the support of the full combined itemset, bread, butter, and jam all together, divided by the support of just the antecedent alone, bread and butter. Equivalently, this can be read as: out of every transaction that contained bread and butter, what fraction of those transactions also happened to contain jam.

Confidence always falls somewhere between 0 and 1. A confidence of 0 means the consequent, jam in this example, was never once present in any transaction that also contained the antecedent, bread and butter. A confidence of 1 means the consequent was present in absolutely every single transaction that contained the antecedent, a perfect, deterministic association within the observed data.
3. Confidence Is Directional

blocks.alt: A implies B is not the same as B implies A

blocks.text: A crucial property that distinguishes Confidence sharply from Support is directionality. The confidence of A implies B is generally a completely different number from the confidence of B implies A, even though the support of the combined itemset A and B together is exactly identical either way, since support does not care about direction at all.

What changes between the two directions is the denominator: confidence of A implies B divides by the support of A alone, while confidence of B implies A divides by the support of B alone instead. If A is a rare item and B is a very common one, A implies B could show high confidence, most transactions with A also contain B, while B implies A shows low confidence, most transactions with B do not contain the rarer A. This directional asymmetry is precisely what makes Confidence a genuinely more informative, and more actionable, metric than Support taken alone.
4. Confidence as Conditional Probability

blocks.alt: Confidence is the conditional probability of B given A

blocks.text: It is worth making an exact mathematical connection explicit here, one that ties directly back to Bayes theorem and conditional probability, first covered in depth in the Naive Bayes topic. Confidence of the rule A implies B is, precisely and without approximation, the conditional probability of B given A, exactly the same mathematical object Bayes theorem and Naive Bayes both work with, just now computed empirically from observed transaction frequencies rather than from a fitted probabilistic model.

This connection is exactly why Confidence feels so naturally interpretable as a measure of directional prediction strength: it is answering the same fundamental question Naive Bayes was built to answer, given this evidence, how likely is that outcome, just phrased here in terms of items in a transaction rather than features and a class label. Recognizing this shared mathematical foundation across seemingly different corners of machine learning is a genuinely useful pattern to keep noticing throughout this course.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Because Confidence is literally a conditional probability, every intuition already built for conditional probability, and for Bayes theorem more generally back in the Naive Bayes topic, transfers directly and exactly to interpreting Confidence values here.

blocks.text: 5. Choosing a Minimum Confidence Threshold

blocks.alt: A high confidence threshold produces stronger, fewer rules

blocks.text: Once frequent itemsets have been found using a minimum support threshold, candidate association rules are typically generated and then filtered a second time, this time using a minimum confidence threshold. This threshold sets how directionally reliable a rule must be, how large a fraction of antecedent-containing transactions must also contain the consequent, before that rule is considered trustworthy enough to report or act on.

Setting this threshold too high means only near-certain, almost deterministic rules survive the filter, which can end up discarding genuinely useful patterns that are strong but not perfectly reliable, for instance a rule that holds 70 percent of the time, which might still be commercially valuable even though it falls short of a 90 percent threshold. Setting the threshold too low lets through a large number of weak, unreliable rules, most of which are not practically actionable and simply add noise to whatever final list of rules is being reviewed or acted upon.

blocks.text: 6. A Concrete Numerical Example

Consider a transaction database with 100 total transactions. Suppose 30 of those transactions contain both bread and butter together, meaning the itemset bread and butter has a support of 0.30. Now suppose that, out of those exact same 30 transactions, 24 of them also happen to contain jam.

The confidence of the rule bread and butter implies jam is then calculated as 24 divided by 30, which equals 0.8, or 80 percent. This is read directly as: among customers who bought both bread and butter together, 80 percent of them also went on to buy jam in that same transaction, a strong, directionally specific, and immediately actionable observation, quite different in character from simply knowing that all three items together have some particular overall support value across the full 100 transactions.
7. Where Confidence Can Mislead

blocks.alt: When B is already very popular, high confidence can be misleading

blocks.text: An 80 percent confidence value sounds genuinely impressive on its own, but it can be seriously misleading without additional context. Suppose jam, entirely independent of whether bread and butter were also purchased, already appears in 78 percent of every single transaction in the entire dataset, simply because jam happens to be an extremely popular, frequently purchased item on its own, regardless of anything else in the basket.

In that case, an 80 percent confidence for bread and butter implies jam is barely better than the 78 percent baseline rate at which jam gets purchased anyway, with or without bread and butter present. The rule, despite its seemingly high confidence, is adding almost no genuine additional predictive information beyond simply knowing how popular jam already is on its own. Confidence, taken by itself, has no built-in way to detect or correct for this problem, since it never looks at the consequent's overall baseline popularity at all. This exact gap is precisely what Lift, the very next topic in this module, was specifically designed to close.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Never trust a high Confidence value in isolation without also checking how common the consequent item already is on its own overall. Lift, covered in the next topic, provides the precise, principled way to make this comparison directly.

blocks.text: 8. Confidence versus Support

blocks.alt: Support measures how common while confidence measures how reliable

blocks.text: It is worth summarizing the distinct role each of these two metrics plays, since they answer genuinely different questions despite both being built from the same underlying transaction counts. Support asks an absolute frequency question: how often does this entire combination of items occur across all transactions, used primarily as an efficient filter for deciding which itemsets are even worth considering as candidates for rule generation in the first place.

Confidence asks a directional, conditional question instead: given that the antecedent already occurred, how reliably does the consequent tend to follow it, used to filter which of the many possible directional rules generated from a frequent itemset are actually strong, reliable, directional predictions worth reporting or acting on. Both metrics are necessary, and neither one alone is sufficient; a genuinely well-designed association rule needs to clear both a minimum support bar and a minimum confidence bar before it is considered worth trusting.

blocks.text: 9. The Standard Pipeline So Far

Putting the last three topics together, the standard association rule mining pipeline now has a clear shape. First, either Apriori or FP-Growth finds every frequent itemset that clears a chosen minimum support threshold, exactly as covered in their own dedicated topics. Second, candidate directional rules are generated from each of those frequent itemsets, exactly as described in the Apriori Algorithm topic's discussion of turning itemsets into rules.

Third, those candidate rules are filtered using a minimum confidence threshold, keeping only the directionally reliable ones, exactly the process covered in this topic. A fourth and final filtering or ranking step, using the Lift metric, remains to be covered in the very next topic, closing the gap this topic just identified: Confidence's blindness to how common the consequent already is on its own.
10. Worked Example

The example below computes Confidence directly for a few candidate rules and demonstrates how the same itemset can produce very different confidence values depending on which direction the rule is stated.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
from mlxtend.frequent_patterns import apriori, association_rules
from mlxtend.preprocessing import TransactionEncoder

transactions = [
    ["bread", "butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter"], ["bread", "milk"],
    ["bread", "butter", "jam", "milk"], ["butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter", "milk"],
    ["bread", "milk"], ["butter", "jam"], ["bread", "butter", "jam"], ["bread", "jam"],
]

encoder = TransactionEncoder()
encoded_array = encoder.fit(transactions).transform(transactions)
df = pd.DataFrame(encoded_array, columns=encoder.columns_)

frequent_itemsets = apriori(df, min_support=0.2, use_colnames=True)
rules = association_rules(frequent_itemsets, metric="confidence", min_threshold=0.0)

# Look specifically at the bread <-> jam pair in both directions
bread_to_jam = rules[(rules['antecedents'] == frozenset({'bread'})) & (rules['consequents'] == frozenset({'jam'}))]
jam_to_bread = rules[(rules['antecedents'] == frozenset({'jam'})) & (rules['consequents'] == frozenset({'bread'}))]

print("bread implies jam:")
print(bread_to_jam[['support', 'confidence']].to_string(index=False))
print("\njam implies bread:")
print(jam_to_bread[['support', 'confidence']].to_string(index=False))
print("\nNotice: identical support, but different confidence values, exactly as this topic explained.")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Both directions of the rule share the exact same support value, since support only depends on the combined itemset, not direction. The confidence values differ because each direction divides by a different single-item support in its denominator, exactly the directionality property covered earlier in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Confidence measures directional prediction strength: given the antecedent occurred, how often did the consequent follow.
It is calculated as the support of the combined itemset divided by the support of the antecedent alone.
Confidence is directional: confidence of A implies B generally differs from confidence of B implies A.
Confidence of A implies B is literally the conditional probability of B given A, the same object underlying Naive Bayes and Bayes theorem.
A minimum confidence threshold filters candidate rules for directional reliability, after minimum support has already filtered itemsets.
High confidence can be misleading if the consequent is already very common on its own, independent of the antecedent.
Support answers an absolute frequency question; Confidence answers a directional, conditional question; both are needed.
The standard pipeline: find frequent itemsets by Support, generate rules, filter by Confidence, then rank or filter by Lift.
Next up: Lift, which corrects Confidence for the consequent's baseline popularity, closing the exact gap this topic identified.
